Security docs and benchmark template to be shared.

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-05
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Liam Chen (Redwood AE), Sofia Ramirez (Redwood SE), Harper Lee (Redwood CSM); Anil Kapoor (VectorHealth Head of AI), Jenna Morris (SRE), Tom Wheeler (Data Eng)

Summary (auto): Align on benchmark plan and harness integration. Discuss streaming vs non-streaming workloads, success criteria, data/scripts to share, and timeline for 3-week POC.

Transcript:
[00:00] Liam Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, appreciate you making time. Quick round of intros, and then we'll jump into the POC scope — specifically the benchmarking harness integration and what we need from you to run a representative load.
[00:18] Anil Kapoor: Yeah hi, Anil here. We're focused on inference costs for our clinical summarization pipeline, and want to validate both latency and throughput with our customer traffic. Jenna, Tom are here for infra details.
[00:29] Jenna Morris: Hey all. We'll mostly be providing network/firewall and traces. Also want to see streaming scenarios because our product streams partial summaries to the UI.
[00:39] Tom Wheeler: Tom here — we'll provide sample scripts, and we have a small harness already, it's more of a wrapper around hey, k6 and some python scripts.
[00:49] Sofia Ramirez: Awesome. So goal for today is to align on success criteria, what scripts/traces you can share, and how Redwood's harness can plug into yours. We'll cover streaming vs non-streaming, plus rough timelines.
[01:03] Liam Chen: Quick note — we've seen customers that need both streaming and non-streaming runs because cost profiles differ a lot when you can early-stop or use prefix caching. Um, so we want to run both.
[01:17] Anil Kapoor: For success criteria: latency p95 under 600ms for the 1k token requests, throughput of at least 30 qps sustained for the non-streaming batch, and cost per 1M tokens comparable to our current provider. If we can't meet those, it's a risk.
[01:34] Sofia Ramirez: That sounds reasonable. Our benchmarking harness supports both streaming (chunked token delivery) and non-streaming full response runs. We can accept your scripts or adapt them into the harness. A few questions about your workload: average tokens per request? distribution? does the request pattern have short tails or lots of long ones?
[01:54] Tom Wheeler: Average is around 650 tokens with a 95th at ~1,200. For streaming cases, we emit tokens as they're produced and the UI consumes them. We can provide a 24-hour trace export.
[02:07] Jenna Morris: And for infra, we need to know what IPs and ports you will use, plus whether we need a VPC peering or we can do an IP allowlist. We prefer VPC peering for security, but can do HTTPS allowlist for the POC.
[02:20] Liam Chen: For the POC we'll support three options: hosted with IP allowlist, dedicated trial in a Redwood Dedicated pool, or private VPC tunnel if you want to test private deployment. For the initial benchmarks, hosted + allowlist is fastest to stand up. Dedicated gives more predictable throughput which is helpful for steady-state numbers.
[02:38] Anil Kapoor: We're leaning toward dedicated for the main runs because we want predictable results that mirror production. But for the integration and quick sanity checks, hosted is fine.
[02:47] Sofia Ramirez: Good. On the harness side, we typically ask for: 1) request-level traces (timestamps, prompt length, streaming or not) 2) sample scripts that reproduce your client behavior 3) expected SLA knobs (p95 target, cold start tolerances). We will convert your scripts into our harness which can then push load via k6 or a ramped runner.
[03:14] Tom Wheeler: Our scripts are Python-based using requests and websockets for streaming. Is websockets supported?
[03:19] Sofia Ramirez: Yes, we support websockets for streaming tests in the harness. There can be some subtle timing differences — the harness will recreate token chunk timing but the network path can affect jitter. We'll annotate results with timestamps so you can correlate.
[03:33] Harper Lee: Also we'll provide a README for the harness integration and an example streaming script.
[03:40] Anil Kapoor: One concern: our data can include PHI. We need to ensure tokens are not stored, logs are encrypted, and we have KMS integration and retention controls.
[03:50] Liam Chen: Absolutely. We'll share our security pack — SOC 2, encryption at rest/transit, KMS options, RBAC controls. For the POC we can enable payload redaction and ensure no logs persist beyond the test window. Harper will share docs after the call.
[04:05] Jenna Morris: Perfect. On measurement: do you report per-token billing during harness runs or a flat metric? We need to model cost.
[04:12] Sofia Ramirez: Our harness records tokens and latency per request. We'll produce a benchmark CSV with token counts, latency quantiles, and inferred cost using Redwood's price spec. If you want, we can run multiple quantization profiles and show the cost/latency tradeoff.
[04:26] Tom Wheeler: Nice. For the non-streaming runs we have batched requests — our client aggregates requests for a short window. Will your runtime support continuous batching + KV cache?
[04:36] Sofia Ramirez: Yes, the runtime supports continuous batching and KV cache. Note that caching benefits vary with prefix reuse — if your requests share a lot of prompt context, you'll see big gains. We'll instrument both with KV cache enabled and disabled so you get apples-to-apples comparisons.
[04:54] Anil Kapoor: About metrics: p50/p95/p99, tokens per second, server CPU/GPU utilization, and end-to-end time as seen by the client.
[05:03] Liam Chen: We'll capture all of those. We can also attach tracing hooks so you can see per-component latency (network, runtime scheduling, token generation).
[05:12] Jenna Morris: On timelines — our infra team can carve out windows next week. How long does Redwood need to set up the dedicated trial?
[05:19] Liam Chen: If we have the scripts and traces by Monday, we can provision a dedicated trial pool by Wednesday and run an initial sanity set by Thursday. Full ramped load tests typically take 2-3 days to configure and validate; then we run the official runs for 1-2 days. So overall 10-14 calendar days from scripts to final report.
[05:39] Anil Kapoor: That's in line with our 3-week target. Good.
[05:44] Sofia Ramirez: A few technical clarifications: 1) streaming vs non-streaming will be separate jobs because the harness handles token chunking differently; 2) for streaming tests we'll simulate client back-pressure; 3) we'll run non-streaming with concurrency levels that match your production QPS and with different batch sizes to see cost/latency curves.
[06:07] Tom Wheeler: For streaming, we also need to test partial-response early stop — sometimes UX cancels after the first chunk. Can the harness simulate early-cancel?
[06:15] Sofia Ramirez: Yes — harness supports early cancellation at configurable token boundaries. We'll run a scenario with 30% early cancel rate to mimic UX behavior.
[06:24] Jenna Morris: Firewall and IP plans: we'll need a list of Redwood egress IPs or a CIDR for the dedicated pool. Also if the trial uses a private VPC we'll need peering details.
[06:35] Liam Chen: We'll provide the IP ranges and, for dedicated trials, a temporary peering config. If VPC is desired we can coordinate support engineering.
[06:43] Anil Kapoor: On success criteria — let's formalize: 1) p95 latency <= 600ms for 1k token non-streaming, 2) sustained throughput >= 30 qps for non-streaming, 3) streaming median latency within 300ms to first token, 4) end-to-end cost within 1.2x of our current provider under equivalent quantization.
[07:01] Liam Chen: We'll aim to measure all four; if any requirement is infeasible we'll call it out and show tradeoffs (e.g., higher quantization lowers cost but may increase p95).
[07:12] Harper Lee: I'll capture those as acceptance criteria and put them in the POC doc.
[07:17] Anil Kapoor: On instrumentation — we need logs that map request id from client to Redwood's request id for correlation. Can you preserve a client-side request id header?
[07:26] Sofia Ramirez: Yes we support passing a request_id header which is returned in logs and traces. We'll include correlation examples in the repo README.
[07:34] Tom Wheeler: About the harness — would you prefer we hand you our python scripts or convert them into k6? We can do either.
[07:41] Sofia Ramirez: Send both if possible. We'll convert python to the harness runners, but k6 is handy for high-concurrency non-streaming. For streaming we prefer the python+websocket approach.
[07:55] Anil Kapoor: Data residency question — our legal asked about EU-only storage. For POC it's okay to use US, but production will need EU region. Does Redwood have EU regions for Dedicated/Private?
[08:05] Liam Chen: Yes, we have EU regions and Dedicated options can be provisioned there. For the POC we can pick the closest region to your users; we will note region in the results.
[08:15] Jenna Morris: One other thing — do you capture GPU-level metrics? We want GPU utilization and kernel timings if possible.
[08:22] Sofia Ramirez: We collect GPU utilization and some scheduler metrics; kernel-level timings are available in some builds and we can enable extra telemetry for the POC. There may be minor noise but it's doable.
[08:34] Anil Kapoor: For the harness outputs — can you provide a CSV and a short PDF summary deck?
[08:40] Liam Chen: Yes, standard deliverables are: CSV with raw samples, an aggregated metrics CSV, and a short results deck with key charts. We'll also include configuration files and the harness commit hash for reproducibility.
[08:52] Tom Wheeler: About replicability: after the POC we'll want to run the harness ourselves against Redwood Dedicated to validate. Will you open-source the harness or provide a private repo?
[09:00] Harper Lee: We'll provide a private repo with instructions; there are parts we can OSS later but for now private access is standard.
[09:08] Anil Kapoor: Any limitations on token lengths or sequence lengths in the trial? We sometimes hit 2k tokens.
[09:15] Sofia Ramirez: Our runtime supports up to 4k tokens in the configured instance type; we can test 2k without issue. For very long sequences we may adjust kernel selection — we'll document which model micro-config was used.
[09:29] Jenna Morris: Ok. On billing, will Redwood provide an estimated cost for the POC runs so we can budget?
[09:35] Liam Chen: We'll run a cost model using your token distribution and our price sheet and share an estimate pre-run. Post-run we'll provide actuals.
[09:42] Tom Wheeler: One of our engineers noted that streaming run patterns often have many small messages which could inflate per-request overhead — will the harness simulate that efficiently?
[09:52] Sofia Ramirez: Yes, the streaming runner uses persistent connections and batched websocket messages to faithfully reproduce that pattern without simulating N separate connections per message. 
[10:04] Anil Kapoor: For the final signoff — we want to see a reproducible run where p95 and throughput meet the criteria and a cost deck. If satisfied we'll discuss Dedicated procurement.
[10:14] Liam Chen: Great. Any other Qs?
[10:17] Tom Wheeler: Small gotcha — our current harness uses a custom retry/backoff. We should align on retry semantics during the test to avoid masking real failures.
[10:27] Sofia Ramirez: Agreed. We'll disable client retries during official runs and only enable them for resilience checks. We'll document the retry settings.
[10:36] Jenna Morris: For networking, we prefer to do an allowlist for the hosted sanity checks and a peered dedicated for the main runs.
[10:44] Liam Chen: Sounds good. We'll send the IP ranges and a peering playbook.
[10:49] Harper Lee: I'll send the SOC2 pack and the harness README right after this call.
[10:56] Anil Kapoor: Timeline recap?
[10:58] Liam Chen: If you provide traces/scripts by Monday (2026-03-09), Redwood will provision by Wednesday (2026-03-11), do sanity checks Thursday-Friday, and run formal load tests the following week with results by end of week, so final report by 2026-03-20. That fits a three-week pilot.
[11:18] Tom Wheeler: Works for us. We'll prioritize the trace export.
[11:22] Jenna Morris: We'll also confirm firewall rules and whether to use allowlist or peering.
[11:28] Anil Kapoor: Thanks everyone. Looking forward to the harness template.
[11:32] Liam Chen: Thanks all. We'll follow up with the repo link and next steps.

Closing notes (auto): Action items captured; next meeting to be scheduled after initial runs if results require deeper tuning.

--END TRANSCRIPT--
